Week 94 Appendix: Half a Minute of Restoration

A week of election interference met a wall of court rulings and a historic midterm sweep that reclaimed oversight power from the executive.

This week combined one of the most significant pro-democratic shocks of the cycle—a decisive midterm election handing Democrats control of both chambers, numerous governorships, and state legislatures—with continuing evidence of executive attempts to subvert electoral integrity before that verdict was rendered. The DOJ's pre-election campaign of threats against election officials, target letters to Democratic lawyers, attempted ballot invalidation in California, and efforts to block Alaska's Senate certification were systematically rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court, demonstrating judicial resilience. Yet Trump's post-election behavior—deflecting blame, staging ballroom and monument spectacles, purging Wiles and DOJ officials, and escalating personalized attacks on critics—suggests continued authoritarian reflexes even as his institutional capacity to act on them narrows. The week's DOJ resignations (Dhillon, Eisenberg, Quiñones) hint at anticipatory retreat ahead of Democratic oversight. Overall, democratic repair mechanisms (elections, courts, resignations under scrutiny) significantly outweighed decay in net effect, though attempted weaponization of federal law enforcement remained severe in degree.

Power and Authority

  1. DOJ threatened criminal prosecution of California election officials who processed contested ballots: Federal prosecutors threatened state election workers with jail time to coerce compliance with a disputed ballot list, testing federal power over state election administration. (2026-11-01)
  2. Trump administration and DOJ filed lawsuit to block certification of Alaska Senate election if Republican candidate lost: The executive branch sought to preemptively override a state's certification of a federal election result, directly threatening the peaceful transfer of power. (2026-11-02)
  3. Mike Dunleavy launched state investigation into alleged Alaska ballot-stacking scheme: A state executive opened a criminal inquiry into alleged campaign tactics during an active election, raising questions about politically timed law enforcement. (2026-11-02)
  4. Trump administration deployed about 1,000 DOJ monitors to polling sites nationwide and considered deploying immigration agents: Large-scale federal deployment to polling places raised concerns about voter intimidation, though no major disruption occurred. (2026-11-01)
  5. Trump delivered Islamophobic attacks on Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at an Iowa campaign rally: A sitting president used a rally to brand a political opponent with hostile religious and ethnic rhetoric, aiming to influence a federal election. (2026-11-01)
  6. Trump publicly attacked voting rights lawyer Marc Elias by name on social media: The president used his platform to brand a private attorney a criminal after a legal defeat, aiming to chill advocacy for voting rights. (2026-11-01)
  7. Essayli continued serving as U.S. Attorney despite a ruling that his appointment was unlawful: An unconfirmed prosecutor kept directing federal law enforcement in election cases, raising constitutional questions about appointment power and oversight. (2026-11-01) [single source]
  8. Trump deflected blame for Republican midterm losses on Truth Social: The president denied responsibility for his party's defeat, affecting public accountability for the election outcome. (2026-11-04)
  9. Trump held a White House ballroom event the day after midterm losses, avoiding substantive acknowledgment of results: The president used a presidential platform to promote a personal construction project rather than address a major electoral rebuke. (2026-11-04)
  10. Trump announced end of military aid to Israel on election day, citing domestic political criticism: A major foreign policy shift was announced as a reaction to electoral messaging, raising questions about policy being driven by political considerations. (2026-11-04)
  11. Trump signed proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments: The president sought to bind future administrations to his personal design choices in the executive residence, an unusual use of proclamation power. (2026-11-06)
  12. Trump removed Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff and replaced her with Stephen Miller: The dismissal of the first female chief of staff, continuing a pattern of ousting senior women, reshuffled top executive leadership after the midterms. (2026-11-06)
  13. DOJ attempted to block election certification and interrupt ballot counting in Alaska and California: Sustained federal legal efforts to override state certification and counting processes represented an escalation of election interference before results were finalized. (2026-11-05)

Institutions and Governance

  1. Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order barring DOJ from threatening election workers over ballot processing: A federal court blocked executive coercion of election workers, protecting the independence of state election administration. (2026-10-31)
  2. Judge Darrin P Gayles dismissed Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice: A federal judge upheld press freedom protections against a presidential attempt to suppress reporting through litigation. (2026-10-31)
  3. Mangione's defense counsel filed motion to dismiss state murder charges on double jeopardy grounds: The filing tests the constitutional limits on parallel federal and state prosecution for the same underlying conduct. (2026-10-31)
  4. Judge Chutkan consolidated District of Columbia v. National Park Service with Lemmon v. Trump: A procedural consolidation streamlined litigation challenging executive approval of a major construction project without congressional authorization. (2026-10-31)
  5. District of Columbia and Commonwealth of Virginia filed complaint challenging National Park Service approval of a commemorative arch: Two jurisdictions sued to test judicial review of administrative procedure and the scope of presidential commemorative authority. (2026-10-31)
  6. Judge Dabney Friedrich dismissed Brown v. Deleeuw and related case Brown v. Trump on removal-power grounds: A federal court upheld a president's removal power over an independent board member while rejecting a Fifth Amendment discrimination claim. (2026-10-31)
  7. Democratic Congress pledged to use budget and oversight authority to constrain Trump's foreign policy: An incoming congressional majority signaled intent to use appropriations and oversight tools to check executive war-making power. (2026-11-01)
  8. Mike Lawler voted against an Iran war resolution and supported a bill expected to cause coverage losses in his district: A congressman's votes on war powers and health insurance became central to voter accountability in a contested district. (2026-11-01)
  9. federal judge (Alaska) dismissed DOJ lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate race: A court rejected an executive attempt to override a state's certification of a federal election, upholding electoral integrity. (2026-11-01)
  10. SCOTUS rejected DOJ appeals seeking to invalidate 20,000 California ballots: The Supreme Court blocked a federal attempt to disenfranchise voters based on an unverified noncitizen list, affirming electoral integrity. (2026-11-01)
  11. Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed charges against two FBI officials accused of lying about the Hunter Biden investigation: A judge found insufficient evidence and criticized prosecutorial timing close to midterms, raising weaponization concerns. (2026-11-01)
  12. Judge William Sullivan heard motion to dismiss murder charges against Lindsay Clancy on double jeopardy grounds: A state court weighed constitutional double jeopardy protections after a deadlocked jury trial. (2026-11-01)
  13. Harmeet Dhillon resigned as head of DOJ Civil Rights Division: The departure of a civil rights division leader who reoriented the office away from protecting minority rights signals institutional change at DOJ. (2026-11-01)
  14. DOJ appealed Ninth Circuit TRO; en banc review granted vacating panel decision on Voting Rights Act private cause of action: Shifting appellate rulings over a key voting rights enforcement mechanism affect the legal tools available to challenge election interference. (2026-11-02)
  15. Douglas DePodesta filed federal lawsuit alleging DOJ pressured him to investigate Trump's political opponents and forced his removal: A former senior FBI official's suit alleges politically motivated prosecutions and retaliation, raising rule-of-law and civil service concerns. (2026-11-02)
  16. Judge Boasberg denied TRO in DSCC v. Trump but granted partial injunction in Trujillo v. DHS against non-citizen ballot demands: Courts split on standing but found the administration likely violated the Elections Clause by directing ballot segregation based on citizenship claims. (2026-11-02)
  17. Judge Tanya Chutkan granted preliminary injunction blocking DHS from disclosing noncitizen voter lists to states: A court found the administration's voter-data transmission policy likely exceeded statutory authority and violated the Privacy Act. (2026-11-02)
  18. Judge Sooknanan denied DOJ's stay request to reinstate a vacated Voter List Maintenance Policy before the election: A court refused to let DOJ revive a rejected policy on the eve of an election, citing arbitrary and capricious rulemaking. (2026-11-02)
  19. Supreme Court denied injunction pending appeal in United States v. California: The Court left a lower court ruling against federal election interference in place pending appeal. (2026-11-02)
  20. Chief District Judge Stephanie M. Rose ordered Iowa to approve a Satanic Temple holiday event at the state capitol: A court protected equal access to a public forum against years of state viewpoint discrimination. (2026-11-03)
  21. SCOTUS rejected Trump administration bid to segregate 20,000 California ballots: The Supreme Court blocked federal interference in state election administration, protecting electoral integrity and federalism. (2026-11-03)
  22. SCOTUS heard oral arguments in St Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on religious exemptions from LGBTQ nondiscrimination rules: A case before the Court could reshape the balance between religious liberty claims and nondiscrimination protections in publicly funded programs. (2026-11-03)
  23. DOJ Civil Rights Division filed status report on removal of sworn officers from election poll-monitoring pool: A court-ordered status report tracked compliance with limits on using law-enforcement personnel as election monitors. (2026-11-03)

  27. House ethics committee investigated Rep. Max Miller for domestic violence and drug use allegations: Congressional ethics oversight scrutinized a sitting member facing serious misconduct allegations during his reelection campaign. (2026-11-04)

  37. Federal judge (Tanya Chutkan) issued a 14-day temporary restraining order halting construction of Trump's triumphal arch: Judicial intervention blocked a major presidential construction project after a commission of administration loyalists had approved it. (2026-11-06) [single source]
  38. Trump appealed his 2024 hush-money conviction to a New York appellate court: The president's effort to overturn a criminal conviction through appellate and immunity arguments tests separation of powers and rule of law. (2026-11-06)

  40. DOJ saw two additional officials resign, including the U.S. Attorney leading an inquiry into Trump's political rivals: The collapse of a politically charged investigation into Trump's rivals followed the resignation of its lead prosecutor ahead of anticipated oversight. (2026-11-06)

  2. FCC requested public comments on a revised NG911 information collection: Modernization of 911 reporting rules affects public safety communications infrastructure and provider compliance obligations. (2026-11-01)
  3. FDA issued final guidance on hepatitis B testing for blood donations: Updated blood-safety testing standards affect public health safeguards and donor screening protocols nationwide. (2026-11-01)
